'''Stuart Alan Rice''' (January 6, 1932 – December 22, 2024) was an American [[theoretical chemistry|theoretical chemist]] and [[physical chemistry|physical chemist]].<ref name="one">[http://chemistry.uchicago.edu/fac/rice.shtml Prof. Rice - Chemistry Department - University of Chicago] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090529032253/http://chemistry.uchicago.edu/fac/rice.shtml |date=2009-05-29 }}</ref> He was well known as a theoretical chemist who also performed experimental research, having spent much of his career working in multiple areas of physical chemistry. He was the Frank P. Hixon Distinguished Service [[Professor]] at the [[University of Chicago]].  During his tenure at the University of Chicago, Rice trained more than 100 Ph.D. students and [[postdoctoral research]]ers.<ref>[http://phdtree.org/scholar/rice-stuart-a/ List of PhDs and Postdocs trained by Professor Stuart A. Rice] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150216052925/http://phdtree.org/scholar/rice-stuart-a/ |date=2015-02-16 }}</ref>  He was elected as member of the [[National Academy of Sciences|National Academy of science]] in 1963. He received the [[National Medal of Science]] in 1999.<ref name="one"/>

==Education and career==
Stuart Rice attended the [[Bronx High School of Science]],<ref name="two">{{cite journal | last=Rice | first=Stuart A. | title=A Fortunate Life in Physical Chemistry | journal=Annual Review of Physical Chemistry | publisher=Annual Reviews | volume=59 | issue=1 | year=2008 | issn=0066-426X | doi=10.1146/annurev.physchem.59.032607.093731 | pages=1–26| pmid=17669016 | bibcode=2008ARPC...59....1R | doi-access= }}</ref> received his [[bachelor's degree]] in 1952 from [[Brooklyn College]], and earned his [[master's degree|master's]] and [[PhD|doctorate]] from [[Harvard University]] in 1954 and 1955, respectively.  He was almost unable to attend graduate school due to contracting [[tuberculosis]], but was cured of the disease through an experimental treatment of [[isoniazid]] and [[streptomycin]].<ref name="two"/>  He remained at Harvard as a junior fellow for three years, although he spent the last two years of the fellowship doing research work at [[Yale University]]'s chemistry department.  After the fellowship, he joined the faculty of [[The University of Chicago]] in 1957, where he remained until his death.<ref name="one"/><ref name="two"/>

Rice served the university in a wide variety of capacities during his fifty-seven year tenure.  He served as the director of the [[James Franck Institute]] (the university's center for [[physical chemistry]] and [[condensed matter physics]]) from 1961 to 1967.  He was chairman of the department of [[chemistry]] from 1971 to 1976 and was dean of the physical sciences division from 1981 to 1995.<ref name="one"/>  He served as dean for the [[Toyota Technological Institute at Chicago]] from October 2006 through October 2010 and as interim president of the institute from October 2010 to April 2013.

In addition to his work at the university, he was on the board of governors at [[Tel Aviv University]],<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.tau.ac.il/bog/members.html |title=Program Members of The Board Of Governors – Tel Aviv University<!-- Bot generated title --> |access-date=7 September 2007 |archive-date=18 August 2007 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070818035942/http://www.tau.ac.il/bog/members.html |url-status=dead }}</ref> served as editor for the journals ''[[Chemical Physics Letters]]''<ref>[http://www.elsevier.com/wps/find/journaleditorialboard.cws_home/505707/editorialboard?navopenmenu=-2 Chemical Physics Letters – Elsevier<!-- Bot generated title -->]</ref> and ''[[Advances in Chemical Physics]]'',<ref>{{Deprecated archive|url=https://archive.today/20121218000440/http://www3.interscience.wiley.com/cgi-bin/bookhome/93517918/ProductInformation.html?CRETRY=1&SRETRY=0|title=Wiley Interscience}}</ref> and co-authored several physical chemistry [[textbook]]s with [[R. Stephen Berry|Stephen Berry]] and [[John Ross (chemist)|John Ross]].<ref>[http://www.oup.com/uk/catalogue/?ci=9780195105896 OUP: UK General Catalogue<!-- Bot generated title -->] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070929120558/http://www.oup.com/uk/catalogue/?ci=9780195105896 |date=2007-09-29 }}</ref>

==Research==
Rice began his scientific career as a high school student and published on this work.<ref>Levine M, Rice SA. 1950. Effect of folic acid, aminopterin and vitamin K on
growth of roots in Allium cepa. Proc. Soc. Exp. Biol. Med. 74:310–12
</ref>  He completed his doctoral dissertation under [[Paul M. Doty|Paul Doty]], contributing to the then-emerging field of [[DNA]] research;<ref name="two"/> the project shared both experimental and theoretical components, which became a hallmark of his later work.<ref name="two"/>

During his time at Yale, Stuart Rice began to study the transport properties of liquids.<ref name="two"/>  He helped to determine the properties of liquid [[noble gas]]es and [[methane]], while also exploring the theoretical background of transport in liquids as well, comparing the results to simulations of [[Lennard-Jones potential|Lennard-Jones fluids]].<ref name="two"/>

Following this work he helped to develop the theory of electronic excitations ([[exciton]]s) in molecular crystals and liquids, eventually moving into the area of radiationless molecular transitions, beginning his own experimental work after the development of the [[Bixon-Jortner model]], while also working with collaborators on extending the theoretical model of these transitions.<ref name="two"/>  This research led him to investigate the effects of [[quantum chaos]] on excited molecules, and to couple the developing model of transitions with quantum chaos in order to attain control of the transition of excited molecules. This led to the field of [[coherent control]], quantum control through [[laser excitation]], which was developed by other scientists at the University of Chicago.<ref name="two"/>

At the same time, he also began work on understanding the electrical properties of [[liquid metal]]s, where the lack of translational orders frustrated attempts to understand their [[electronic band structure]].<ref name="two"/>  The discrepancy between the dielectric results of [[reflectivity]] and [[ellipsometry]] data of liquid mercury led to work on the nature of [[electrical conductivity|conductivity]] at the liquid-vapor surface of liquid metal, ultimately showing that the existence of [[ion]] inhomogeneities at the interface led to electronic changes in the bulk liquid that persist for several [[atom]]ic diameters into a liquid.<ref name="two"/>

Stuart became immersed in the theory of freezing,<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Bagchi |first=Biman |last2=Cerjan |first2=Charles |last3=Rice |first3=Stuart A. |date=1983-12-01 |title=Contribution to the theory of freezing |url=https://pubs.aip.org/jcp/article/79/11/5595/446946/Contribution-to-the-theory-of-freezing |journal=The Journal of Chemical Physics |language=en |volume=79 |issue=11 |pages=5595–5604 |doi=10.1063/1.445680 |issn=0021-9606|url-access=subscription }}</ref> which evolved to the study of quasi two-dimensional liquids.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Zangi |first=Ronen |last2=Rice |first2=Stuart A. |date=2004-01-22 |title=Cooperative Dynamics in Two Dimensions |url=https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRevLett.92.035502 |journal=Physical Review Letters |language=en |volume=92 |issue=3 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.92.035502 |issn=0031-9007|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

In 1985, Stuart A. Rice, [[David Tannor|David J. Tannor]], and [[Ronnie Kosloff]] introduced a new approach to the active control of molecular dynamics. They demonstrated theoretically that the branching ratios of competing chemical reactions could be controlled using a carefully timed sequence of ultrashort laser pulses, known as the '''pump–dump scheme<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Tannor |first=David J. |last2=Kosloff |first2=Ronnie |last3=Rice |first3=Stuart A. |date=1986-11-15 |title=Coherent pulse sequence induced control of selectivity of reactions: Exact quantum mechanical calculations |url=https://doi.org/10.1063/1.451542 |journal=The Journal of Chemical Physics |volume=85 |issue=10 |pages=5805–5820 |doi=10.1063/1.451542 |issn=0021-9606|url-access=subscription }}</ref>'''. The first pulse (pump) creates a vibrational wavepacket on an excited electronic potential-energy surface. After a controlled period of evolution, the second pulse (dump) transfers the wavepacket back to the ground electronic state, directing the reaction toward a desired product channel. This theoretical proposal was subsequently validated by experimental demonstrations. Stuart Rice subsequently helped consolidate the time-dependent and time-independent approaches to [[coherent control]], identifying quantum coherence as their common underlying principleIe.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Rice |first=Stuart A. |date=1992-10-16 |title=New Ideas for Guiding the Evolution of a Quantum System |url=https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.258.5081.412 |journal=Science |language=en |volume=258 |issue=5081 |pages=412–413 |doi=10.1126/science.258.5081.412 |issn=0036-8075|url-access=subscription }}</ref>  

Stuart Rice proposed with M. Demirplak<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Demirplak |first=Mustafa |last2=Rice |first2=Stuart A. |date=2005-04-01 |title=Assisted Adiabatic Passage Revisited |url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/jp040647w |journal=The Journal of Physical Chemistry B |language=en |volume=109 |issue=14 |pages=6838–6844 |doi=10.1021/jp040647w |issn=1520-6106|url-access=subscription }}</ref> that a counter adiabatic control field that can force a system to follow an adiabatic path in a finite time, establishing a framework known as [[shortcuts to adiabaticity]], which has since become widely used in quantum technologies.

Smaller research topics that Rice published on include work on the chemistry of water, the theory of freezing liquids, the properties of monolayers on liquids, and confined [[colloid]]al systems, amongst others.<ref name="two" />

==Personal life and death==
Rice was famous at the [[University of Chicago]] for eating lunch almost every weekday at the university's [[Quadrangle Club (University of Chicago)|Quadrangle Club]] restaurant (a faculty club), where he dined over 9,000 times.  Rice was known to sit at the head of the chemistry table, not because he was the most senior member of the department, but because he was very tall.<ref>[http://magazine.uchicago.edu/0506/features/club.shtml The University of Chicago Magazine<!-- Bot generated title -->]</ref>

Rice was married to Marian Coopersmith from 1952 until her death in 1994.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Fleming |first1=Graham R. |last2=David |first2=Oxtoby |title=Tribute to Stuart A. Rice |journal=The Journal of Physical Chemistry |volume=99 |issue=9 |date=2 March 1995 |pages=2413–2434 |doi=10.1021/j100009a600 }}</ref> From 1997 to his own death, Rice was married to Ruth O'Brien. He died on December 22, 2024, at the age of 92.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Stuart Rice Obituary (1932 – 2024) - Legacy Remembers |url=https://www.legacy.com/us/obituaries/legacyremembers/stuart-rice-obituary?id=57078124 |access-date=2024-12-24 |website=Legacy.com}}</ref>

==Honors and awards==
Rice was awarded the [[National Medal of Science]], the highest scientific prize awarded in the United States, in 1999. He was awarded the [[Wolf Prize]] in Chemistry in 2011, along with [[Krzysztof Matyjaszewski]] and [[Ching W. Tang|Ching Tang]].<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.wolffund.org.il/cat.asp?id=15&cat_title=CHEMISTRY |title=The 2011 Wolf Prize in Chemistry |access-date=16 February 2011 |archive-date=17 May 2007 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070517203044/http://www.wolffund.org.il/cat.asp?id=15&cat_title=CHEMISTRY |url-status=dead }}</ref> He was a Fellow of both the [[United States National Academy of Sciences|National Academy of Sciences]] and the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]]<ref>{{Cite web |title=Stuart A. Rice |url=https://www.nasonline.org/directory-entry/stuart-a-rice-2xsipe/ |access-date=2022-05-12 |website=www.nasonline.org}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Stuart Alan Rice |url=https://www.amacad.org/person/stuart-alan-rice |access-date=2022-05-12 |website=American Academy of Arts & Sciences |language=en}}</ref> and a member of the [[American Philosophical Society]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=APS Member History |url=https://search.amphilsoc.org/memhist/search?creator=Stuart+Alan+Rice&title=&subject=&subdiv=&mem=&year=&year-max=&dead=&keyword=&smode=advanced |access-date=2022-05-12 |website=search.amphilsoc.org}}</ref> In 1970, Rice was awarded the Llewellyn John and Harriet Manchester [[Quantrell Award]] for Excellence in Undergraduate Teaching, the nation’s oldest prize for undergraduate teaching, a highly esteemed faculty award at [[University of Chicago|The University of Chicago]].<ref name="one"/>

==Impact==
Over the course of his long career Rice has shaped much debate on theoretical physical chemistry.  He is cited on the National Medal of Science "for changing the very nature of modern physical chemistry through his research, teaching and writing, using imaginative approaches to both experiment and theory that have inspired a new generation of scientists."<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nsf.gov/od/nms/recip_details.cfm?recip_id=290 |title=The President's National Medal of Science: Recipient Details &#124; NSF - National Science Foundation |publisher=Nsf.gov |date=2000-03-14 |access-date=2020-02-22}}</ref>  With over 100 [[doctoral]] students to his credit, Stuart Rice has had a great impact on the field of physical chemistry simply through the number of research scientists he has trained.<ref>[http://chronicle.uchicago.edu/050526/maclean.shtml Rice, Straus to receive Maclean<!-- Bot generated title -->]</ref> Theoretical chemist [[David Tannor]], who is the Hermann Mayer Professorial Chair in the department of chemical physics at the [[Weizmann Institute of Science]] in Israel, did his post-doc work with Stuart Rice and [[David W. Oxtoby]] at the University of Chicago.<ref name="auto3a">[http://www.weizmann.ac.il/chemphys/tannor/home "David Tannor's Home Page; Highlights of Research,"] Weizmann Institute of Science, Department of Chemical Physics.</ref><ref name="autoa">{{Cite web|url=http://www.israel21c.org/can-safed-become-israels-aspen/|title=Can Safed become Israel's Aspen?|first=Sharon|last=Kanon|date=June 15, 2007|website=Israel21c}}</ref><ref name="auto2a">{{Cite web|url=https://www.uscibooks.com/tannor.htm|title=Introduction to Quantum Mechanics, A Time Dependent Perspective, David Tannor|website=www.uscibooks.com|access-date=22 February 2020|archive-date=19 November 2002|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20021119014530/https://www.uscibooks.com/tannor.htm|url-status=dead}}</ref> [[Paul Alivisatos]], president of University of Chicago, who studied with Rice as an undergraduate, remembers his teaching as "exact and illuminating and inspiring. As long as he continued to speak, he rendered his difficult subject with simplicity and clarity."<ref>{{Cite web |title=A teacher’s legacy |url=https://mag.uchicago.edu/university-news/teachers-legacy |access-date=2025-06-25 |website=mag.uchicago.edu |language=en}}</ref>
